title: Harvey Power Users: Building the Culture — Andrei Salajan at Schoenherr
author: Harvey Team · Andrei Salajan

dom.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supplies only headings on document review and legal AI governance, with no substantive claims, evidence or recommendations showing whether it accepts or rejects the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Salajan reinforces the cluster’s agentic-workflow and operating-model thesis by identifying a concrete capability-building mechanism: sustained hands-on use develops the power users who can design and build multi-step legal agents. His account also strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on adoption and deliberate training, though it is experiential and predictive rather than quantified evidence of workflow or business-model outcomes.
qs: Training sessions help with the fundamentals, but real progress comes from hands-on use.

As we move into an [agentic framework](/agents) — where AI doesn't just respond to prompts but executes multi-step workflows autonomously — the power users who invested the time to understand how AI thinks will be the ones designing and building those agents.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Salajan accepts that access and raw prompt volume are insufficient, and materially develops the cluster’s proposition with an organisational framework combining hands-on practice, continuing upskilling, peer ambassadors, feedback loops and client collaboration. His account supports sustained engagement as an initial value signal while distinguishing power users through purposeful experimentation and knowledge sharing; however, it offers practitioner observations rather than measured productivity outcomes.
qs: Evolve is what we build on top of it — moving from “are people using the tools” to genuinely reshaping how we work, how we develop our people, and how we collaborate with clients on what AI makes possible.
Training sessions help with the fundamentals, but real progress comes from hands-on use.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that value comes from organisational redesign rather than usage volume and materially extends the cluster with a concrete adoption model: layered technology, upskilling, client collaboration, power-user experimentation and ambassador-led peer diffusion. It offers implementation experience rather than evidence of measured productivity or ROI.

kp.k: Hands-on change management underpins reported strong AI adoption
kp.d: In this Harvey-published interview, Salajan reports that Schoenherr supported early Harvey adoption by establishing a baseline, educating lawyers, setting expectations and explaining limitations, then continuing training as features developed. He describes this approach as comparatively successful against other law-firm transformation efforts, without providing adoption rates or a quantified comparison.
qs: We took a very hands-on approach to change, establishing a baseline, educating people on what the technology can do, setting expectations, and being clear about limitations.
That was surprisingly successful compared to other transformation efforts in law firms.
We had a very strong baseline on early adoption and we always built on that, training and implementing the latest features.

kp.k: Power-user identification extends beyond prompt volume
kp.d: Salajan says the firm initially identified power users through double or triple the number of prompts, interpreting sustained engagement by skeptical lawyers as a signal of value. He also emphasizes complex-feature use, experimentation, feedback and sharing best practice. These are his interpretations of observed usage patterns, rather than quantified measurements of work quality or productivity.
qs: At the beginning, it was fairly simple: we looked at usage and identified people running double or triple the number of prompts.
So when you see consistent engagement, that's the first signal they're getting something out of it.
Power users are the ones using new, more complex features, delivering feedback, and constantly pushing our tools to their limits.
They're creative and share best practice within the firm.

kp.k: Evolve links technology, upskilling and client collaboration
kp.d: Salajan describes Schoenherr's Evolve framework as moving beyond tool uptake toward reshaping work, professional development and collaboration with clients. Its three pillars combine a layered technology stack, upskilling and collaboration with technology partners and clients; the interview describes the framework's direction rather than measured downstream outcomes.
qs: The bigger picture is a framework we call Evolve, built on three pillars: a strategically layered technology stack, a future-ready upskilling programme, and deep collaboration with technology partners and clients.

Evolve is what we build on top of it — moving from “are people using the tools” to genuinely reshaping how we work, how we develop our people, and how we collaborate with clients on what AI makes possible.

kp.k: Ambassadors spread adoption through peer examples and feedback
kp.d: Salajan describes a Legal Tech Club of around 50 ambassadors who receive early feature access and participate in special projects in exchange for substantial feedback. He attributes cross-practice interest to peers showcasing success stories and creating competition between practice groups. He also reports that power-user feedback helped shape Harvey's product.
qs: The Legal Tech Club is one recent example — a group of around 50 ambassadors who get early access to features and work with us on special projects.
In return, we expect a high level of feedback on the solutions.
It's not just the legal tech team telling people what's possible; it's about bringing in the right people to showcase their own success stories.
That creates a healthy sense of competition between practice groups, where teams start to think, "If they're doing this, we should be taking a closer look too."
We got early feedback from our power users and constantly contributed to shaping the product and delivering feedback to Harvey.

kp.k: Dedicated sessions encouraged early use of review features
kp.d: Salajan reports that Schoenherr pushed early adoption of Harvey's Vault and tabular review features, prioritizing them while some other firms waited. Dedicated sessions and active encouragement were the stated implementation measures; he does not report task-level performance results from their use.
qs: While some firms waited, we saw the potential immediately and prioritised
We ran dedicated sessions and actively encouraged teams to start using them right away.

kp.k: Time investment matters more than initial technical confidence
kp.d: Salajan says existing document-automation and transaction-management power users had an easier starting point, but identifies time, rather than skepticism, as the main constraint. He reports a correlation between time invested and becoming a power user, distinguishes foundational training from hands-on learning, and presents willingness to invest time as the condition for bringing users along.
qs: We already had legal tech power users before AI, in areas like document automation and transaction management, and those individuals weren't intimidated by new tools or interfaces.
The biggest limitation isn't skepticism, it's time.
We saw a clear correlation between people investing time and becoming power users.
Training sessions help with the fundamentals, but real progress comes from hands-on use.
We haven't seen anyone we couldn't bring along, as long as they're willing to invest the time.

kp.k: AI itself can support learning and troubleshooting
kp.d: Salajan argues that AI differs from earlier technologies because users can ask the system how to prompt and why something is not working. He presents recognizing this interactive learning capability as a potentially significant shift in users' development.
qs: It's the first technology where the system itself helps teach you how to use it.
How do I write a prompt? It shows you. Why isn't something working? It helps you understand.
Once people grasp that, the shift can be significant.

kp.k: Agentic workflows could widen capability gaps between users
kp.d: Salajan predicts that users who invest deeply in understanding AI will become designers and builders of agents executing multi-step workflows autonomously. He expects the gap between deeply engaged and less-engaged users to widen as the technology evolves. This is a forward-looking claim, with no specified timeline or measured evidence of that future role transition.
qs: where AI doesn't just respond to prompts but executes multi-step workflows autonomously
the power users who invested the time to understand how AI thinks will be the ones designing and building those agents.
The gap between someone who engaged deeply and someone who didn't is only going to widen.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Salajan claims that hands-on change management and peer-led collaboration support strong legal-AI adoption and provide a foundation for changing how a firm works.
pts.d: Andrei Salajan, Schoenherr’s Director of Legal Tech & Digitalisation, attributes strong Harvey adoption to establishing a baseline, educating lawyers, setting expectations about limitations, and continuing training as features develop. He describes the Evolve framework as moving beyond tool usage toward reshaping work, staff development and client collaboration. Its Legal Tech Club uses approximately 50 ambassadors to test features, supply feedback and share successes, which he says stimulates competition and interest across practice groups. The broader changes are presented as the programme’s direction, rather than quantified completed outcomes.

pts.k: Salajan interprets sustained, sophisticated AI use as a signal that lawyers obtain value, not merely as high activity.
pts.d: He says early power users could be identified by running double or triple the number of prompts, but distinguishes usage volume from deeper engagement: exploring complex features, providing feedback, testing limits and sharing practices. He attributes continued engagement to perceived value for skeptical lawyers; he does not specify measured time savings, output quality improvements or financial returns.

pts.k: Salajan claims AI can help teach users how to use it, making invested time and hands-on engagement central to developing expertise.
pts.d: He describes AI’s ability to assist with prompting and troubleshooting as a distinctive change from earlier legal technologies. Prior technical interest makes entry easier, but he identifies time rather than skepticism as the largest constraint. He reports a correlation between time invested and becoming a power user, and says his team has been able to bring along everyone willing to invest that time.

pts.k: Salajan predicts that experienced AI users will design autonomous multi-step agents and that the capability gap with less-engaged users will widen.
pts.d: He anticipates a transition from prompt-response interaction to AI executing multi-step workflows autonomously. He predicts that users who invested time in understanding AI will become the people designing and building those agents. This is a future role and capability prediction, not a reported deployment outcome or a claim that lawyers will be replaced.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw primarily on Salajan’s experience managing adoption at Schoenherr, with limited descriptive usage information and no reported formal outcome study.
pts.d: Salajan cites observed prompt volumes, patterns of advanced feature use, feedback, training experience and an approximately 50-person ambassador group. His claimed correlation between time investment and expertise is not accompanied by a dataset, measurement method or statistical results. No adoption percentage, productivity benchmark, legal-quality assessment or client-outcome measure is supplied. The agent-design and widening-gap claims are predictions extrapolated from that experience. The source is a Harvey company-blog interview published as part of its power-user research; the linked RSGI feature is not reproduced as supporting evidence in the supplied text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Adoption and learning claims concern experience up to the May 12, 2026 interview; agent-related changes are prospective and undated.
pts.d: Salajan describes early Harvey adoption followed by ongoing training, feature implementation and a recent ambassador initiative, without providing start dates or observation periods. Strong adoption is described as the foundation for Evolve’s wider changes. Development into a power user is conditional on willingness and time for practical engagement, while prior technical familiarity eases the starting point. The prediction about agent builders and a widening capability gap is conditional on the move toward agentic workflows, with no deadline or quantified rate of change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Schoenherr’s lawyers, practice groups and legal-tech team, with clients included in the intended collaborative changes.
pts.d: Lawyers develop differing levels of AI proficiency; deeply engaged users share practices and are predicted to become agent designers. Practice groups are encouraged to adopt features through peer examples and competition. The legal-tech team manages education, early access and feedback, while ambassadors help shape implementation and contribute product feedback to Harvey, the software provider. Clients are included in Evolve’s collaboration pillar, but the interview identifies no concrete client savings or service-quality outcomes. It makes no specific prediction about headcount, billing, legal-market shares or access to justice.
